segments.translation: Once again the venerable [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} sets out that same meaning, through the contemplation of a [game of dice]{dyuta}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} setting out that same meaning once again, through the contemplation of a [game of dice]{dyuta}. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) says instead that he speaks in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of gambling (cp.12.m1).

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has dyūtakrīḍādhyānena, 'through the contemplation of a game of dice', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rgyan po 'gyed pa dgongs pa'i skad kyis, 'in the twilight (intentional) language of gambling'. Its manuscript may have read a word for twilight language (sandhyā-) where Shastri's text has dhyāna. I translate the Sanskrit.
Munidatta names the poet kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ (honorific plural). I render it with the glossary's 'Kāṇha' and 'the venerable' for -pāda; see questions.

segments.translit: karuṇeti| svādhiṣṭhānacittarūpaṃ cittaṃ boddhavyaṃ| pi[hā]ṛīti| tasyāśrayasaptadoṣāḥ samādhimalā boddhavyāḥ| tān phāṭayitvā nirāsīkṛtya nayaṃ mantranayarahasyaṃ caturthānandabalaṃ tameva bodhicittaṃ vajragurorupadeśāt samyak kuliśājasaṃyogena ubhayorekatayā aviratānandābhiyogena krīḍāṃ kurvvan bhavabalaṃ viṣayābhāsabalaṃ akleśavaśena asmābhiḥ kṛṣṇacāryyairjitamiti|
segments.translation: '[Compassion]{karuna}': this is to be understood as the [mind]{citta}, in the form of the [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} mind. '[Pihāṛi]{pihari}': this is to be understood as the seven faults of its support, the stains of [samādhi]{samadhi}. Having split them and cast them out, and playing the game with naya, the secret of the [way of mantra]{mantranaya}, with the strength of the fourth [joy]{ananda}, that very [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, by the [instruction]{upadesa} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}, through the proper union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, through the oneness of the two, through uninterrupted application to [joy]{ananda}: so the [forces of existence]{bhavabala}, that is, the force of the [appearance]{abhasa} of [sense objects]{visaya}, have been conquered by me, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, free from the sway of the [afflictions]{klesa}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the game's [compassion]{karuna} as the [mind]{citta} in [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} form, and [pihāṛi]{pihari} as seven faults staining [samādhi]{samadhi}, which are removed. Playing with [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} in union, by the [guru]{guru}'s instruction, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} conquers the force of the appearance of [sense objects]{visaya}, free from the [afflictions]{klesa}' sway; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'by the power of the afflictions' (cp.12.m2).

equations.en: the mind, in the form of the self-blessing mind
the seven faults of its support, the stains of samādhi
the secret of the way of mantra
the force of the appearance of sense objects

flags.note: akleśavaśena: I read a-kleśa-vaśa, 'free from the sway of the afflictions'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nyon mongs pa'i dbang gis, 'by the power (vaśa) of the afflictions', without the negative, as if reading kleśavaśena; that would suit the way of great passion (freed by passion itself). The note records the difference.
akleśavaśena could also be the idiom akleśa, 'without trouble', giving 'effortlessly'. The Tibetan's dbang for vaśa supports my reading 'sway'.

The Tibetan's lemma for pihāṛi is rgyal, 'victory' (its line has rgyal mtshan, 'banner'), and it adds a sentence the Sanskrit lacks: de rnams las rgyal ba ni dmigs pa med ces bya'o, 'victory over them is called non-apprehension'. It also attaches the gloss 'the secret of the way of mantra, the strength of the fourth joy' to rgyan po, 'the (dice) game', not to naya.

nayaṃ mantranayarahasyaṃ caturthānandabalaṃ tameva bodhicittaṃ is a string of accusatives. I take it as the song's naa bala taken up word by word: naya glossed 'the secret of the way of mantra', and bala taken up in 'the strength of the fourth joy', both identified with bodhicitta and serving as objects of the play (as in the song's 'I play naa bala').

tasyāśrayasaptadoṣāḥ: 'the seven faults of its (the mind's) support', or 'the seven faults based on it'; the Tibetan de'i rten ting nge 'dzin gyi sgrib pa skyon bdun puts 'its support' in apposition to the obscurations of samādhi. Munidatta does not list the seven.
kuliśāja- is apparently for kuliśābja-, 'vajra and lotus'; the Tibetan rdo rje dang chu skyes confirms 'lotus'.
asmābhiḥ kṛṣṇācāryaiḥ is the honorific plural, 'by us, Kṛṣṇācārya', with Munidatta paraphrasing in the poet's voice; rendered 'by me, Kāṇha' to match the song's first person.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena spaṣṭayannāhuḥ—
phīṭetyādi| prathamameva vajrajāpakrameṇa ābhāsadvayaṃ phīṭamiti niḥkṛntitaṃ| punaḥ ṭhakuramavidyācittaṃ upakārikopadeśeneti| rāgānte[20] viramānandodayasamaye bodhicitākṣaropadeśena aviratānandena kṛṣṇācāryyasya jinavara[sya] svayameva sannidhāna[mā]gatya militamiti|
tathāca daṛatīpādāḥ—
rāgānte viramapraveśasa[ma]ye candre svabhāvasthite(ti)
yā citti(ti)rmanasaḥ pravṛttiraparā vāyornni[ru]ddhā gatiḥ|
tatkāle yadananyasambhavasukhaṃ sākṣāt paraṃ tatpadaṃ
tatra svānubhavo hi yasya sa punaḥ siddho mahāmudrayā||
segments.translation:
Making it plain with the [refrain]{dhruvapada}, he says: 'The two are cut off…' and so on. First of all, by the process of [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, the pair of [appearances]{abhasa} is cut off: phīṭa means severed. Then 'the [king]{thakura}': the [mind]{citta} of [ignorance]{avidya}; 'by the helper's [instruction]{upadesa}'. At the end of [passion]{raga-passion}, at the time when the [joy of cessation]{viramananda} arises, through the [instruction]{upadesa} on imperishable [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, through uninterrupted [joy]{ananda}, it came of itself into the presence of [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, the best of [Jinas]{p-jina}, and was united with him.
And so [Daṛatīpāda]{p-darati} says:
At the end of [passion]{raga-passion}, at the moment of entering cessation, when the [moon]{moon} rests in its own [nature]{svabhava},
there is the awareness that is the mind's activity, and, besides, the stilled course of the [wind]{vayu}.
At that time the [bliss]{sukha} that arises nowhere else is, directly, that supreme state.
Whoever has his own experience of it there is accomplished through [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain's two as the pair of [appearances]{abhasa}, cut off by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, and the [king]{thakura} as the mind of [ignorance]{avidya}. When the [joy of cessation]{viramananda} arises, something unnamed comes of itself to [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) makes it the king's palace. A quoted verse of [Daṛatīpāda]{p-darati} calls that moment's [bliss]{sukha} the supreme state (cp.12.m3).

citations.quoted: rāgānte viramapraveśasamaye candre svabhāvasthite … tatra svānubhavo hi yasya sa punaḥ siddho mahāmudrayā ("At the end of passion, at the moment of entering cessation … is accomplished through Mahāmudrā")
citations.work: a verse of Daṛatīpāda, as Munidatta attributes it; he does not name the work

flags.note: kṛṣṇācāryyasya jinavara[sya] svayameva sannidhānam āgatya militam: with Shastri's restored -sya the neuter militam has no subject, so I render 'it came … and was united with him'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nag po spyod pa rgyal po'i pho brang rang nyid kyis nye bar …, 'the king's palace itself (came) near Kṛṣṇācārya', echoing its line 2b rgyal ba'i pho brang, 'the Jina's palace' (the song's jinaura, 'city of the Jina'). That points to jinapuram, which would give militam its subject: 'the city of the Jina came of itself near Kāṇha and was reached'. The Tibetan verb nye bar 'joms looks corrupt (perhaps for nye bar 'ongs, 'came near').

punaḥ ṭhakuram avidyācittaṃ upakārikopadeśena iti has no verb: 'the king, the mind of ignorance', then the song's 'by the helper's instruction' (taāri uesa). He may mean that the king is cut off by the helper's instruction. The Tibetan construes ma rig pa'i sems la phan par byed pa po'i thabs kyis, 'by the means of the one who benefits the mind of ignorance'.

Where the Sanskrit has aviratānandena, 'through uninterrupted joy', the Tibetan has khyad par gyi dga' bas, 'through the joy of cessation', as if reading viramānandena; in cp.12.m2 the same translators render avirata- as rgyun mi 'chad pa.

bodhicitākṣaropadeśena: akṣara taken as 'imperishable', as the Tibetan byang chub kyi sems mi 'gyur ba, 'unchanging bodhicitta', has it; 'the instruction in the syllables of bodhicitta' is also possible.

In Daṛatīpāda's verse the Tibetan has no moon: bsams pa yis ni rang bzhin gnas par byed, 'by thought one makes (it) abide in its own nature'. It renders aparā as gzhan yang, 'moreover', which I follow ('besides'), and ends phyag rgya chen po'i dngos grub sgrub pa'i phyir, 'in order to accomplish the siddhi of Mahāmudrā'. It names the author u Da'i zhabs.

Shastri's parenthetic corrections svabhāvasthite(ti) and citti(ti) are left aside: I read candre svabhāvasthite as a locative absolute ('when the moon rests in its own nature') and citti as 'awareness'.
siddho in the verse is the participle 'accomplished', so I did not render it with the glossary's noun 'siddha'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsātiśa[ya]kramatāṃ kathayanta(ṃmā) āhuḥ—
pahilemityādi| vaṛiketi sandhyābhāsayā ṣaṣṭyuttaraśataprakṛtayo vajrajāpakrameṇa prathame niḥsvabhāvīkṛtya punarapi gaavareṇeti yogīndrasya tathatācittagajendreṇa pañcaskandhātmakapañcaviṣayasyāhaṃkāramamakārādibhūṣaṇaṃ praha(hā)tya nirmmadaḥ kṛtvā sākṣātkṛtamiti|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada}, setting out the gradual heightening of practice, he says: 'First…' and so on. '[Pawns]{baria}' (vaṛikā): in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti}. Having first made them [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava} by the process of [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, then again, 'by the fine [elephant]{elephant}', that is, by the [mind]{citta} of [suchness]{tathata} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, that lord of [elephants]{elephant}, having struck down the ornament of [I-making and mine-making]{ahamkara-mamakara} and the rest that belongs to the five [sense objects]{visaya}, which consist of the five [aggregates]{skandha}, and having made them free of pride (nirmada): it was directly realized.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [pawns]{baria} as the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti}, first made [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava} by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, and the fine [elephant]{elephant} as the mind of [suchness]{tathata} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, which strikes down the [I-making and mine-making]{ahamkara-mamakara} adorning the five [sense objects]{visaya}. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends with [selflessness]{nairatmya} directly realized (cp.12.m4).

equations.en: the hundred and sixty natures (in twilight language)
the mind of suchness of the lord of yogis, as lord of elephants

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit ends nirmmadaḥ kṛtvā sākṣātkṛtam, 'having made (them) free of pride, it was directly realized' (with no object for 'realized'), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag med pa mngon sum du byed pa, 'makes selflessness directly manifest', as if its manuscript named selflessness (nairātmya) as what is realized. The note records this.
praha(hā)tya: I translate the printed prahatya, 'having struck down'. Shastri's (hā) and the Tibetan rab tu spangs nas, 'having thoroughly abandoned', point to prahāya, 'having given up'.
nirmmadaḥ (nominative) with kṛtvā is awkward; nirmadaṃ, 'having made (it) free of pride', is probably meant.
nirmada also describes an elephant out of rut (mada, 'ichor'), which fits the elephant image; whether Munidatta intends the play is not clear, so I give the plain sense 'free of pride'.

The Tibetan renders ahaṃkāra-mamakāra as dar byed pa dang bdag tu byed pa (dar perhaps a slip for ngar, 'I') and bhūṣaṇa as rgyan po, the word it uses for the dice game in cp.12.m1 and m2. It takes the five aggregates and the five objects as a pair (phung po lnga'i bdag nyid dang yul lnga'i) rather than 'five objects consisting of the five aggregates'.
kathayanta(ṃmā) carries Shastri's parenthetic correction; the sense, 'setting out … he says', is not affected.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena taṃ dyotayanta āhuḥ—
matiemiti| matyā prajñāpāramitānubuddhyā| ṭhakuramiti saṃkleśāropitacittaṃ parinirvvā(20ka)ṇāropitaṃ kṛtaṃ| ataeva bhavabalaṃ bhāvagrāmabalaṃ rūpādiviṣayaṃ| suvyagrasamagraṃ kṛtvā jitamasmābhiḥ|
tathāca nāgārjjunapādaiḥ—
yena cittena te bālā saṃsāre bandhanaṃ gatāḥ|
yoginantena cittena sugatānāṃ gatiṃ gatāḥ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada}, making that plain, he says: 'By [intelligence]{mati}': by intelligence, that is, by understanding that follows the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}. 'The [king]{thakura}': the [mind]{citta} on which [affliction]{klesa} had been superimposed is made one on which [parinirvāṇa]{parinirvana} is superimposed. For this very reason 'the [forces of existence]{bhavabala}' are the force of the host of things, the [sense objects]{visaya} beginning with form. Having thrown them all into utter confusion, I have conquered them.
And so the venerable [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} says:
The mind by which those fools have gone into [bonds]{bandhana} in [saṃsāra]{samsara}:
by that same mind [yogis]{yogi} have gone to the state of the [sugatas]{sugata}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads [intelligence]{mati} as understanding that follows the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}, and the [king]{thakura} as the [mind]{citta}, on which [parinirvāṇa]{parinirvana} is now superimposed instead of [affliction]{klesa}. The [forces of existence]{bhavabala} are the host of things, the [sense objects]{visaya}. He quotes [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna}: the mind that binds fools in [saṃsāra]{samsara} brings [yogis]{yogi} to the [sugatas]{sugata}' state (cp.12.m5).

equations.en: understanding that follows the perfection of wisdom
the mind on which affliction had been superimposed, made one on which parinirvāṇa is superimposed
the force of the host of things, the sense objects beginning with form

citations.quoted: yena cittena te bālā saṃsāre bandhanaṃ gatāḥ | yoginas tena cittena sugatānāṃ gatiṃ gatāḥ ("The mind by which those fools have gone into bonds in saṃsāra: by that same mind yogis have gone to the state of the sugatas")
citations.work: a verse of Nāgārjuna, as Munidatta attributes it; he does not name the work

flags.note: suvyagrasamagraṃ kṛtvā, which answers the song's abaśa kariā ('making him helpless'): vyagra can mean 'bewildered, thrown into disorder' or 'busy, occupied'. I take 'having thrown them all into utter confusion'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang gi brel ba mtha' dag byas pas, roughly 'having made all of it one's own business', as if reading sva- for su- and taking vyagra as 'busy'; its sense is unclear.

For āropita, 'superimposed', the Tibetan has bskyed pa, 'produced': nyon mongs pas bskyed pa'i sems yongs su mya ngan las 'da' bar skyed par byed pa, 'the mind produced by the afflictions is made to produce parinirvāṇa'.

For matyā prajñāpāramitānubuddhyā the Tibetan has blo gros shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin mar reg par bya'o, 'intelligence is to touch the perfection of wisdom'; for bhāvagrāma, 'host of things', it has dngos po'i grong, 'town of things', taking grāma in its sense 'village'.
yoginantena in the verse stands for yoginas tena; the Tibetan (rnal 'byor sems de nyid kyis ni) agrees with that reading.
jitam asmābhiḥ, honorific plural in the poet's voice, rendered 'I have conquered', as in cp.12.m2.

segments.translit:
caturthapadenātmano yogāspadasyānuśaṃsāmāhuḥ(ha)—
bhaṇa ityādi| kṛṣṇācāryyohi vadati dāyaṃ prābhṛtā[ti]śayābhiprāyaṃ catuḥṣaṣṭikoṣṭake nirmmāṇacakre sthirīkṛtya svacittaṃ prakṛtiprabhā[sva]rarūpaṃ gṛhṇāmi| 12||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of his own station in yoga: '[Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says…' and so on. For [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: 'The [move]{daha} (dāya, a gift) is the intention of an exceptional offering. Making it [steady]{sthira} in the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra} with its sixty-four [squares]{kotha}, I take my own [mind]{citta}, whose form is by nature [clear light]{prabhasvara}.'
segments.note: Munidatta renders the good [move]{daha} as dāya, a gift, meaning the intention of an exceptional offering; the sixty-four [squares]{kotha} are those of the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}, where [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, making it steady, takes his own [mind]{citta}, [clear light]{prabhasvara} by nature. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'the intention of a thought of the real as it is' instead (cp.12.m6).

equations.en: the intention of an exceptional offering

flags.note: prābhṛtā[ti]śayābhiprāyaṃ: Shastri's restored [ti] gives 'the intention of an exceptional offering', which I translate. Without it the manuscript reads prābhṛtāśaya-, 'the thought of an offering'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yang dag pa ji lta ba'i bsam pa'i dgongs pas, 'by the intention of a thought (āśaya) of the real as it is', which supports āśaya and seems to read (yathā)bhūta, 'real', in place of prābhṛta, 'offering'.

Munidatta renders the song's dāha as dāya, 'gift', and his gloss (an offering) depends on that sense. I kept the glossary's 'move' for daha and added 'dāya, a gift' so the gloss makes sense; see questions.
The Tibetan's lemma is bde mchog, 'supreme bliss', as in its line 5a (bdag ni bde mchog bzang), not a word for a move or a gift.
sthirīkṛtya has no expressed object; it may be the mind (svacittaṃ) or the offering. I keep 'making it steady'.
prakṛti here is 'by nature' (prakṛtiprabhāsvara, 'clear light by nature'), not the glossary's prakṛti, 'natures', of cp.12.m4, so it is not marked.

questions: Munidatta names the poet Kṛṣṇācārya(pāda) throughout; following the glossary I rendered it [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} ('the venerable Kāṇha' for -pāda). Should 'Kṛṣṇācārya' be a listed variant of p-kanha for the commentary, so his own form of the name can stand?

cp.12.m6: Munidatta renders the song's dāha as dāya, 'gift', and builds his gloss (an offering) on that sense. I kept the glossary's 'move' and added '(dāya, a gift)'. Should daha list 'gift' as a variant for the commentary, or should dāya be left unmarked?

cp.12.m3: Shastri restores jinavara[sya], which leaves militam without a subject; the Tibetan rgyal po'i pho brang ('the king's palace', matching its 'Jina's palace' for the song's jinaura) points to jinapuram, 'the city of the Jina'. I translated Shastri's text and flagged it. Should the translation follow the Tibetan here?

cp.12.m2: akleśavaśena ('free from the sway of the afflictions') against the Tibetan nyon mongs pa'i dbang gis ('by the power of the afflictions'), which lacks the negative and would fit the way of great passion. I followed the Sanskrit; please confirm.
cp.12.m6: keep Shastri's restored [ti] ('exceptional offering')? The unrestored prābhṛtāśaya- and the Tibetan ('a thought of the real as it is') both point to āśaya, 'thought, disposition'.

Several keep-source-first-gloss terms first appear here in the commentary (bodhicitta, samādhi, vajra, Mahāmudrā, sugata). The weave schema gives each segment one note, which I used for Munidatta's reading, so they have no gloss note. Should the woven notes carry these glosses, or are the glossary links enough?
